title: Home Sharing and Short-Stay Hosting
desc: Plan, run and review a safe, legal and honest short-stay home, from first listing to repeat guests.
outcomes: Explain the local rules, safety duties and guest expectations for a short-stay home.
Prepare a compliant listing, house manual and turnover checklist.
Compare nightly price, occupancy and costs to find true profit per month.
Judge guest reviews and fix the three most common complaints.
Launch a full hosting plan with pricing, calendar, safety and guest journey.
task: Prepare and run one short-stay home (or room) for a 30-day pilot with a complete listing, house manual, safety checks, pricing sheet and guest review log.
condition: A real room or home you may legally share (or a practice case supplied by your mentor), a phone, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. About 8 weeks part-time.
standard: Written permission or rule check is on file; every safety item passes the checklist; price covers costs with a margin you can show; the guest review average and complaint log are recorded honestly; peers rate the evidence Meets or better.
who: Home owners, tenants with permission, property caretakers, small hosts, hospitality trainees and returners.
req: none; you must have the right to host or use the practice case
evidence: rules check, listing, house manual, safety checklist, pricing sheet, 30-day guest log
modules: Is hosting right for you, and are you allowed?
Understand
Hosting is a small business inside a home. Before photos or prices, confirm that you are allowed to host and that your household agrees.
Check three things: owner or landlord permission, building or society rules, and local registration, tax and safe-stay rules.
Ask the household: noise, shared spaces, privacy, who cleans, who greets guests.
Write a one-page go or no-go note with the rule you checked and the date.
A tenant in a flat finds the lease bans sub-letting. She writes to the owner, receives written permission for short room stays, files the paper, and only then takes photos. Go decision dated 3 March.
Write your go or no-go note with three rules checked and one household agreement.
Give each rule a source (document or office) and a date, and write no guess as a fact.
Knowing your guest
Analyse
A listing wins when it fits a real guest: a worker on a short job, a family visiting relatives, a student on an exam trip.
Read 10 public listings near you; record price per night, what is promised, and what guests praise or complain about.
Pick one main guest type and write three needs (quiet, kitchen, near transport).
Write a promise you can keep every time.

Ten listings near a hospital show most complaints are about noise and late check-in. The host chooses visiting relatives as guests and promises: quiet after 9 pm, self check-in from 2 pm, a kettle and a tea set.
Build your table of 10 listings and your one-line promise.
Show price with currency in the table, and write a promise that is specific and testable by a guest.
Safety first
Apply
A pleasant stay is a safe stay. Safety items are not optional extras.
Fit and test smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms where relevant; show exits; keep a first-aid box and emergency numbers on the wall.
Check electrics, gas, locks, stairs, balcony rails and water heating; log the date and who checked.
Protect guest privacy: tell guests about any cameras at the door and never place them inside rooms.
A host tests the alarm on 5 May, finds a dead battery, replaces it and writes the new date on the checklist. A loose stair rail is tightened and photographed before the next guest.
Complete the safety checklist for your space and attach photos of each fix.
Check that all items pass, give every fix a date, and confirm there are no hidden cameras anywhere in guest areas.
The listing and honest photos
Create
Words and photos are a promise. Honest, bright and specific beats fancy.
Title: place type, area, one benefit. Description: the first three lines answer who, where, what is included.
Photos: daylight, tidy, each room, outside entrance, and the view from the bed. No editing that hides flaws.
List house rules kindly and clearly: quiet hours, smoking, visitors, check-in and check-out.
Weak title: "Lovely home". Strong title: "Quiet room 8 minutes from the hospital, own bath, self check-in". The description ends with: "Street is busy until 8 pm; the room faces the garden."
Write the title, a 120-word description, a photo list of 12 shots and five house rules.
Describe the stay so that a stranger can picture it, and promise nothing that you cannot deliver.
Pricing and true profit
Evaluate
Price is not what you hope for; it is what covers cost, fits the market and leaves a margin.
Costs per month: cleaning, laundry, power, water, internet, supplies, platform fee, tax, repairs, your time.
Break-even nights = monthly cost divided by profit per night. Compare to realistic occupancy from your 10 listings.
Use weekday, weekend and long-stay prices; review every two weeks.

Costs are 18,000 INR a month; a nightly price of 2,000 INR leaves 1,300 INR profit after cleaning (an estimate; check your market). Break-even is 14 nights. The area average is 12 nights, so the host raises the long-stay discount carefully and watches for 30 days.
Build a monthly sheet with all costs, three prices and break-even nights; write the currency next to every number.
Calculate sheet totals correctly and compare break-even with real local occupancy.
The guest journey: before, during, after
Apply
Guests judge the whole journey, not only the room.
Before: a welcome message, directions, check-in time, rules. During: a quick check-in message and one way to reach you. After: thanks, a review request and lost-items check.
Self check-in must be secure: change codes every guest and never share master keys.
A turnover checklist: strip, wash, clean, restock, test, photo, lock.

A guest arrives late; the host's directions include a photo of the gate and a phone number. Next morning the host sends a 2-line message: "Everything ok? Tell me by 10 am." The guest reports a slow shower; fixed that day.
Write your four standard messages and a turnover checklist.
Write polite messages, under 60 words each, that name one clear action.
Reviews, problems and fairness
Evaluate
Problems will happen. Fair, calm replies protect your name and the guest.
Answer every review within two days: thank, state facts, say what you changed.
For damage or disputes, keep dated photos and messages; use the platform process; stay respectful.
Treat all guests equally; never refuse a guest for protected reasons such as race, faith or disability (check what your local rules protect), and never discriminate.
A guest writes that the towels were thin. The host replies: "Thank you; we replaced the towels with new ones on 12 May." The next three reviews mention clean, soft towels.
Write replies to two real or practice reviews and a one-page problem protocol.
Write replies that are factual, polite and show a change; name in the protocol who does what within 24 hours.
Pilot, measure and improve
Create
Run a 30-day pilot and turn data into a better stay.
Log nights booked, income, costs, guest scores and complaints.
Fix the top 3 complaints; repeat what guests praise.
Write a 90-day plan: price, calendar, upgrades, and one sustainability step such as saving water or helping a neighbour start hosting.
After 30 days: 11 nights booked, average score 4.6 of 5, top complaint is hard-to-find entrance. A sign and a new photo are added; the next 5 guests find it with no call.
Present your pilot log and 90-day plan to your peer circle.
Use real numbers with matching totals, and date three fixes and one improvement plan.
quiz: Name three checks before you list a home.
Permission (owner or landlord), building rules, and local registration, tax and safety rules.
Why must cameras never be inside guest rooms?
It breaks privacy and is unlawful in many places and always a breach of trust; check the local rule, and use only a declared door camera outside.
Define break-even nights.
Monthly cost divided by profit per night: the number of nights you must book to cover your cost.
Give two items on a safety checklist.
Smoke alarm tested, gas or electrics checked, first-aid box, exits shown, stair rails safe.
What belongs in the first three lines of a listing?
Who the stay suits, where it is, and what is included.
How do you handle a poor review?
Reply within two days with thanks, facts and what you changed.
Why change door codes for every guest?
It keeps the home secure and guests safe.
Name one fair-treatment rule.
Treat guests equally; never refuse for race, faith, disability or another protected reason.
What do you log in a 30-day pilot?
Nights, income, costs, guest scores and complaints.
Why write the currency next to every number?
Readers in other places cannot compare or check numbers without it.
rubric: Complete with dated fixes and photos
Journey tested and improved from reviews
jobs: Runs a home or rooms for guests
Cleans, restocks and inspects between guests
Grows from one room to several
next: customer service and communication, hospitality operations, bookkeeping for small business.
local: Short-stay rules differ by city: registration, tax, night limits and building rules change. Check yours first and write the source next to each rule.
